blocks.content: Have you ever booked a flight online?
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245780338-7f3293d4.png
You do not call each of those systems yourself. You just click one button. That button is the Facade.
A design pattern that hides the complexity of a system and provides a single, simple interface to the client.
This is exactly what the Facade Pattern does in code.
Imagine your app needs to place an order. Without a facade, your client code has to do all of this itself:
Five different subsystems.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245780579-de2c11a8.png
Now add a Facade:

// With Facade - client calls one thing
orderFacade.placeOrder(productId, userId, address);

blocks.content: One call. Everything handled. The client does not need to know what happens inside.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245780792-4fd5a419.png

• Your system has many interdependent components that need to work together.
  • Clients should not need to understand internal complexity.
  • You want one clean entry point instead of scattered subsystem calls.
Let's walk through a real example and see how it works.
1. The Problem: Online Order Complexity
Let's say you are building an online shopping app.
On the surface, placing an order seems simple. But behind the scenes it involves a sequence of coordinated steps:
["Check if the product is in stock","Process the customer's payment","Generate an invoice","Send a confirmation email"]
items: Check if the product is in stock

blocks.content: Each of these steps is handled by a separate class with its own API.
Order Subsystems
1. Inventory Service
2. Payment Service
3. Invoice Service
4. Email Service

blocks.content: Client Code Without Facade
Without a facade, the client must talk to every subsystem directly knowing exactly which methods to call and in what order.

codes.python:
class InventoryService:
    def check_stock(self, product_id):
        print(f"Inventory: Checking stock for product {product_id}")
        print("Inventory: Product is available.")
        return True

    def reserve_item(self, product_id):
        print(f"Inventory: Reserving item {product_id}")
        print("Inventory: Item reserved successfully.")


class PaymentService:
    def process_payment(self, user_id, amount):
        print(f"Payment: Processing ${amount} for user {user_id}")
        print("Payment: Payment approved.")
        return True


class InvoiceService:
    def generate_invoice(self, user_id, product_id, amount):
        import time
        invoice_id = f"INV-{int(time.time() * 1000)}"
        print(f"Invoice: Generating invoice {invoice_id}")
        print(f"Invoice: Invoice created for ${amount}")
        return invoice_id


class EmailService:
    def send_confirmation(self, user_id, invoice_id):
        print(f"Email: Sending confirmation to user {user_id}")
        print(f"Email: Confirmation sent. Invoice: {invoice_id}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    user_id = "USR-001"
    product_id = "PRD-42"
    amount = 149.99

    # Client must create and manage all subsystems
    inventory = InventoryService()
    payment = PaymentService()
    invoice = InvoiceService()
    email = EmailService()

    print("--- Placing Order ---")

    # Step 1: Check stock
    if not inventory.check_stock(product_id):
        print("Order failed: Product out of stock.")
        exit()

    # Step 2: Process payment
    if not payment.process_payment(user_id, amount):
        print("Order failed: Payment declined.")
        exit()

    # Step 3: Reserve the item
    inventory.reserve_item(product_id)

    # Step 4: Generate invoice
    invoice_id = invoice.generate_invoice(user_id, product_id, amount)

    # Step 5: Send confirmation
    email.send_confirmation(user_id, invoice_id)

    print("Order placed successfully!")

blocks.content: Now imagine placing an order from three different places a web controller, a mobile API, and a scheduled retry job. You would have to duplicate this entire sequence every single time.
What's Wrong With This Design?
The client is directly interacting with multiple subsystems, making the system complex, tightly coupled, and hard to maintain.
1. High Client Complexity
The client must know every subsystem, every method, the correct order, and every failure condition. This is way too much responsibility for a client class.
2. Tight Coupling
The client directly depends on all four services. Change one method signature anywhere and every client that places orders breaks.
3. Poor Maintainability
Want to add a loyalty points system? A fraud check? A SMS notification? You have to update every single place that places orders duplicating logic and introducing inconsistency.
4. Difficult Testing
Testing the client means mocking four different subsystems and setting up the entire sequence for every single test case.
What We Need

• Hide the complexity of all four subsystems behind one simple interface.
  • Let the client place an order with a single method call.
  • Keep all orchestration logic in one place so changes only happen once.
  • Make the system easy to test, extend, and maintain.
This is exactly where the Facade Pattern fits in.
2. The Facade Design Pattern

The Facade Pattern provides a single, simplified interface to a complex system that contains multiple subsystems. Instead of the client dealing with many different classes and method calls, it interacts with one high-level object (the Facade) which internally coordinates everything.
Real-World Analogy
Imagine staying at a luxury hotel. As a guest (the client), you could call housekeeping for extra towels, the restaurant to book a table, and valet service to bring your car.
But instead of contacting each department separately, you simply call the Front Desk Concierge (the Facade).
You might say:
"Please arrange dinner for me at 8 PM and have my car ready afterwards."
The concierge then communicates with the restaurant, valet, and other hotel services (subsystems) to complete your request.
From the guest’s perspective, everything happens through one simple point of contact, while the internal coordination remains hidden.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245781601-4b8c3856.png
Components in the Facade Pattern
The Facade pattern consists of three main components that together simplify interaction with complex subsystems while keeping the system modular and maintainable.
1. Facade (Example: DeploymentFacade)
The Facade understands which subsystem classes are required and the correct sequence in which they should be used.
It exposes a simple method for the client while internally delegating work to different subsystems.
2. Subsystem Classes (Example: VersionControlSystem, BuildSystem)
Subsystem classes contain the actual implementation and business logic for individual tasks.
They operate independently and do not depend on the facade, meaning they can still be used directly if needed.
3. Client (Example: Main Application or Script)
The client interacts only with the Facade instead of calling each subsystem individually.
This greatly simplifies the client code and reduces dependency on internal system details.
3. Implementing the Facade
The CoffeeMachineFacade class serves as a single, unified interface to everything involved in making a cup of coffee.
Internally it holds references to four simple components:
["Grinder Grinds the coffee beans","Heater Heats the water to the right temperature","Brewer Brews the coffee","Cup Pours the final drink"]
items: Heater Heats the water to the right temperature

blocks.content: Instead of forcing the client to call each of these in the right order, the facade wraps it all into one method: makeCoffee().
How It Works
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245781804-e5c5529e.png
The client makes one call. The facade handles every step inside. If heating fails, it stops early. The client never knows which part went wrong.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245782066-c97e6097.png
The Facade Class
The client does not touchGrinder,Heater,Brewer, orCupdirectly. It simply callsmakeCoffee()and gets coffee.

blocks.content: Tomorrow the machine gets new features:
["makeLatte(milkType) brew with steamed milk","makeIcedCoffee() brew over ice","cleanMachine() run a cleaning cycle"]
You just add new classes behind the scenes MilkSteamer, IceTray, CleaningCycle and expose them as new methods on the facade.

Clients that only want basic coffee keep callingmakeCoffee()and never see the new parts. Clients that want lattes get a clean new method. The machine can grow as complex as it needs to the facade keeps the outside simple and stable.
4. Practical Example: Restaurant Order System
Imagine you walk into a restaurant and tell the waiter "I'd like pasta please."
Behind the scenes the waiter tells the chef to cook it, the kitchen manages inventory, the billing system calculates the price, and the delivery staff brings it to your table.

Without a facade, every part of your app the table app, the waiter's handheld device, the online order portal needs to coordinate all of those steps manually. A RestaurantFacade wraps it all into placeOrder() and closeTable().
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245782237-6dd27fb1.png
Facade
Client

The client does not know who cooked the food, how inventory was managed, or how billing works. It just places the order and closes the table. If you later add a loyalty points system or a kitchen display screen, you update the facade every client gets the new behaviour automatically.
